questions.title: Antigenic drift is caused by mutation
questions.question: Antigenic drift of viruses is caused by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Recombination is an exchange of genetic sequence between two related genomes, a different mechanism from the point mutations that drive drift.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reassortment (exchange of whole genome segments) is the mechanism behind antigenic shift, not drift, and it requires a segmented genome that drift does not.
explanations.C: Correct. Antigenic drift is a gradual change in a virus's surface antigens caused by the accumulation of point mutations in the genes encoding those surface proteins, most classically described for influenza's hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. It is a slow, continuous process that can occur in any virus with a mutable genome, unlike antigenic shift, which is abrupt and confined to segmented-genome viruses. This is why influenza vaccines require near-annual reformulation to keep pace with drift.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reassortment plays no role in drift specifically; combining it with mutation misattributes the mechanism of antigenic shift to drift.

questions.learning_objective: State that antigenic drift is caused by the gradual accumulation of point mutations, distinct from antigenic shift's reassortment mechanism.

questions.title: Nucleocapsid-only virus is naked
questions.question: Viruses that consist of only a nucleocapsid are considered?

explanations.A: Correct. A naked (non-enveloped) virus consists of the nucleocapsid only -- genome plus capsid -- with no surrounding lipid envelope, in contrast to an enveloped virus, whose nucleocapsid is additionally wrapped in a host-membrane-derived envelope. Naked and non-enveloped are synonyms for this same structural fact. This structural difference is why naked viruses are generally more resistant than enveloped viruses to lipid solvents, detergents and drying.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An incomplete (defective) virus is missing one or more genes needed for independent replication; that describes a genetic deficiency, not the presence or absence of an envelope.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Simple virus" is not a standard structural category in virology and does not name the nucleocapsid-only arrangement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A viroid is an uncoated circular RNA molecule with no capsid or envelope at all, not a nucleocapsid (genome plus capsid) as described here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a naked (non-enveloped) virus as one consisting of the nucleocapsid only, with no envelope.

questions.title: Parvoviridae is the ssDNA exception
questions.question: All the following families contain dsDNA EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Polyomaviridae carries double-stranded DNA, so it belongs with the other dsDNA families listed and is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Poxviridae carries double-stranded DNA (and, unusually, replicates in the cytoplasm), so it is not the exception here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Papillomaviridae carries double-stranded DNA, consistent with the other dsDNA families listed.
explanations.D: Correct. Parvoviridae is the single-stranded DNA exception among DNA virus families -- while Polyomaviridae, Poxviridae and Papillomaviridae are all double-stranded, Parvoviridae is the one DNA family whose genome is single-stranded. This makes it the standard "odd one out" answer whenever a list of DNA virus families is presented and asked which is NOT double-stranded. Parvovirus is also, separately, the smallest DNA virus known.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Parvoviridae as the single-stranded DNA exception among dsDNA virus families.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: DNA viruses replicate in nucleus, RNA viruses in cytoplasm
questions.question: In general, most DNA viruses multiply in the host cell's _____, while most RNA viruses multiply in the host cell's _____?

explanations.A: Correct. As a general rule, DNA viruses assemble and replicate in the host cell's nucleus, where host DNA polymerase and other nuclear machinery are available, while RNA viruses replicate in the host cell's cytoplasm. Poxvirus is the standard exception on the DNA side, replicating entirely in the cytoplasm because it encodes its own complete replication machinery. This nucleus-vs-cytoplasm rule is a foundational fact for predicting where a given virus's inclusion bodies or cytopathic changes will appear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cell membrane is not the site of DNA virus replication, and this pairing does not match either the DNA-virus or RNA-virus rule.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the correct pairing; the general rule places DNA viruses in the nucleus and RNA viruses in the cytoplasm, not the other way round.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neither the cytoplasm-for-DNA-viruses nor the cell-membrane-for-RNA-viruses half of this pairing matches the general teaching rule.
explanations.E: Incorrect. RNA viruses generally replicate in the cytoplasm, not the endoplasmic reticulum specifically, even though the nucleus-for-DNA-viruses half is correct.

questions.learning_objective: State the general rule that DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus and RNA viruses in the cytoplasm, with poxvirus as the DNA-virus exception.

questions.title: Fungal cell membrane contains ergosterol
questions.question: Fungal cell membrane contains?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, not the fungal cell membrane.
explanations.B: Correct. The fungal cell membrane's characteristic sterol is ergosterol, the fungal counterpart of the cholesterol found in animal cell membranes. This structural difference is the basis of antifungal drug selectivity: azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis and polyenes bind ergosterol directly, targets absent from human cell membranes. Ergosterol is a membrane lipid, distinct from chitin, which is instead a cell-wall polysaccharide.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chitin is a structural polysaccharide of the fungal cell wall, not a membrane lipid, so it does not answer a membrane-composition question.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cholesterol is the characteristic sterol of animal cell membranes, not fungal ones; fungi use ergosterol instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that ergosterol, not cholesterol, is the fungal cell membrane's characteristic sterol.

questions.title: Opportunistic fungal infection risk factors
questions.question: Factors contributing to the initiation of opportunistic fungal infections include each of the following EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS a risk factor). Fungi are classically controlled by T-cell-mediated immune responses, so defective cell-mediated immunity predisposes to opportunistic fungal infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS a risk factor). Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic use disrupts the competing normal bacterial flora, allowing fungal overgrowth.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a risk factor). Chemotherapy is both immunosuppressive and neutropenic, both of which predispose to opportunistic fungal infection.
explanations.D: Correct. Anaerobic wound conditions are instead a classic predisposing factor for anaerobic bacterial infection (for example gas gangrene caused by Clostridium species), not for opportunistic fungal infection, so this is the one factor that does NOT belong on the list. Defective cell-mediated immunity, prolonged antibiotic use and chemotherapy are all genuine predisposing factors for opportunistic fungal infection. This item tests the distinction between bacterial-infection risk factors and fungal-infection risk factors, which are frequently confused on exams.

questions.learning_objective: List defective cell-mediated immunity, prolonged antibiotic use and chemotherapy as opportunistic-fungal-infection risk factors, and recognize anaerobic wound conditions as a bacterial (not fungal) risk factor.

questions.title: Prions are infectious protein particles
questions.question: Protein particles which can infect are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A virion is a complete virus particle, consisting of a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein capsid -- it always contains nucleic acid, unlike the protein-only particle described here.
explanations.B: Correct. A prion is an infectious protein particle that contains no detectable nucleic acid of any kind -- it is protein-only. Because it lacks nucleic acid, a prion cannot replicate the way a virus does; instead it propagates by inducing a conformational (misfolding) change in the host's own normal cellular protein. Prions are responsible for transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nucleoid is the irregular region of a prokaryotic cell containing its DNA, not an infectious protein particle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Prions" correctly names an infectious protein particle, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify prions as infectious protein particles.

questions.title: Herpesvirus structure
questions.question: Which one of the following is about Herpes viruses?

explanations.A: Correct. Herpesviruses are classified as icosahedral-symmetry, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses. This structural profile underlies their characteristic biology, including the ability to establish latency in host cells after primary infection. This combination distinguishes them from RNA viruses (which have a different genome type), from non-enveloped DNA viruses, and from complex-symmetry, brick-shaped viruses such as poxvirus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Polyhedral" is not the standard term used for herpesvirus capsid symmetry, which is specifically icosahedral.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Herpesviruses are DNA viruses with icosahedral symmetry, not RNA viruses with helical symmetry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Brick shape" (complex symmetry) describes poxviruses, not herpesviruses, whose capsid symmetry is icosahedral.

questions.learning_objective: State that herpesviruses are icosahedral, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Bacteriophages parasitize bacteria
questions.question: The viruses that live as parasites on bacteria are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fungi are not viruses at all, so they cannot be the virus category described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Commensal" describes a relationship of an organism with its host (living together without harming it), not a category of virus that infects bacteria.
explanations.C: Correct. A bacteriophage (phage) is, at its most basic definition, a virus that lives as a parasite specifically on bacteria, infecting and often lysing them. Bacteriophages are used as tools in molecular biology and can also mediate horizontal gene transfer between bacteria (for example transduction). They are the specific term for a virus whose host is a bacterium, distinguishing them from viruses that infect animal or plant cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Bacteriophages" is the correct, standard term, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State the basic definition of a bacteriophage as a virus that parasitizes bacteria.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Virus contains DNA or RNA
questions.question: Virus will contain?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A virus has no cell membrane of its own; that is a structure of true cells, not viruses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A virus has no cell wall; a cell wall is a structure of bacterial, fungal or plant cells, not viruses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "DNA" alone is too narrow, since a virus's genome may instead be RNA; the correct, complete answer must allow for both possibilities.
explanations.D: Correct. Every virus carries exactly one type of nucleic acid as its genome -- either DNA or RNA -- and never both together, one of the defining structural features separating viruses from cellular organisms. A virus has no cell membrane or cell wall of its own; its only universal structural components are its nucleic acid genome and the capsid surrounding it. This single-nucleic-acid-type rule underlies the basic DNA-virus/RNA-virus classification used throughout virology.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus's genetic material is either DNA or RNA, never both, and that it has no cell membrane or cell wall.

questions.title: Poxvirus is the largest virus
questions.question: The Largest virus is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parvovirus is in fact the smallest virus among the commonly tested families, the opposite extreme from what is asked here.
explanations.B: Correct. Among medically important viruses, poxvirus (for example vaccinia) is the largest, at roughly 200-450 nm, large enough to be visible even by light microscopy. This size, together with its complex capsid symmetry, distinguishes it from smaller, simpler-symmetry virus families. Poxvirus's large genome also lets it encode its own complete cytoplasmic replication machinery, unlike most other DNA viruses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rhabdovirus (bullet-shaped) is a mid-sized virus, not the largest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Pox virus" is the correct answer, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify poxvirus as the largest virus among the commonly tested virus families.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Parvovirus is the smallest virus
questions.question: The smallest virus is?

explanations.A: Correct. Parvovirus is the smallest virus among the commonly tested families, at roughly 18-26 nm, among the smallest DNA viruses known -- consistent with it also being the ssDNA exception among DNA virus families. Its small genome size limits it to encoding relatively few proteins, so parvoviruses depend heavily on host-cell machinery, more so than larger DNA viruses do. Poxvirus, by contrast, is the largest virus, anchoring the opposite end of the viral size range.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhabdovirus (bullet-shaped) is mid-sized, not the smallest virus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Poxvirus is in fact the largest virus, the opposite extreme from what is asked here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adenovirus is a mid-sized, non-enveloped icosahedral DNA virus, not the smallest.

questions.learning_objective: Identify parvovirus as the smallest virus among the commonly tested virus families.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Virion is the extracellular infectious particle
questions.question: The extra cellular infections virus particle is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The capsid is only the protein coat surrounding the genome, one component of the complete extracellular particle, not the whole particle itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nucleocapsid is the genome plus capsid together, but for an enveloped virus the complete extracellular particle also includes the envelope, which "nucleocapsid" alone does not capture.
explanations.C: Correct. A virion is the complete, extracellular, infectious virus particle -- for a naked virus, the nucleocapsid alone; for an enveloped virus, the nucleocapsid plus its surrounding envelope. This is the unit that a plaque assay or hemagglutination test ultimately counts when quantitating viral titer. The term specifically denotes the fully assembled, infectious particle outside a host cell, as opposed to viral components still being assembled inside one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Virion" is the correct, standard term, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a virion as the complete extracellular infectious virus particle.

questions.title: HIV belongs to Retroviridae
questions.question: HIV is belonging to?

explanations.A: Correct. HIV belongs to the family Retroviridae, and as such it is correctly described both as an RNA virus and, more specifically, as a retrovirus. The defining feature of all retroviruses, including HIV, is reverse transcriptase, an RNA-directed DNA polymerase that copies the viral RNA genome into DNA before integration into the host chromosome. This classification underlies HIV's characteristic biology, including chronic proviral integration into the host genome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhabdoviridae (bullet-shaped, includes rabies virus) is an unrelated RNA virus family, not HIV's family.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Togaviridae (includes rubella and alphaviruses) is an unrelated RNA virus family, not HIV's family.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Paramyxoviridae (includes measles and mumps viruses) is an unrelated RNA virus family, not HIV's family.

questions.learning_objective: Classify HIV as a member of the family Retroviridae.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Retrovirus hallmark: reverse transcriptase
questions.question: Special feature of Retro viruses?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (only half-correct). Reverse transcriptase names the enzyme, which is correct, but by itself this option omits that reverse transcriptase and "RNA-directed DNA polymerase" are simply two names for the same enzymatic activity.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (only half-correct). "RNA-directed DNA polymerase" correctly describes the enzyme's activity, but this option alone omits its common name, reverse transcriptase.
explanations.C: Correct. Reverse transcriptase and RNA-directed (RNA-dependent) DNA polymerase are two names for the same defining retroviral enzyme, which copies the virus's RNA genome into DNA before integration into the host chromosome. This is the special, hallmark feature that distinguishes retroviruses from all other RNA virus families, none of which reverse-transcribe their genome. Detecting this enzyme's activity in a patient's blood is used clinically as a marker of retroviral (including HIV) infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Boils" is not a virology term and does not describe any retroviral feature.

questions.learning_objective: State that reverse transcriptase, an RNA-directed DNA polymerase, is the special hallmark feature of retroviruses.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: AIDS virus is a retrovirus
questions.question: AIDS virus is?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. HIV is indeed an RNA virus, but "retrovirus" is the more specific, complete classification intended here, since a retrovirus is itself a particular kind of RNA virus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. HIV's genome is RNA, not DNA (though its provirus, after reverse transcription, does integrate as DNA into the host chromosome).
explanations.C: Correct. HIV, the AIDS virus, is a retrovirus -- an RNA virus of the family Retroviridae whose defining feature is reverse transcriptase, an RNA-directed DNA polymerase that copies its RNA genome into DNA for integration into the host chromosome. "Retrovirus" is the specific, complete classification that captures both its RNA genome and its distinctive reverse-transcription biology. This is the answer that best matches how HIV is standardly classified in medical microbiology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enteroviruses (for example poliovirus, coxsackievirus) are an unrelated picornavirus genus, not HIV's classification.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the AIDS virus (HIV) specifically as a retrovirus.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: HIV blood marker: reverse transcriptase
questions.question: Following is the marker of HIV infection in blood?

explanations.A: Correct. Detecting reverse transcriptase activity in a patient's blood serves as a laboratory marker of retroviral, including HIV, infection, because reverse transcriptase is the hallmark enzyme HIV (and all retroviruses) uses to copy its RNA genome into DNA before host-chromosome integration. This assay was historically important for HIV diagnosis and research before more modern molecular and antigen/antibody tests became standard. It reflects HIV's specific retroviral biology rather than a feature shared with ordinary RNA or DNA viruses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordinary DNA polymerase is a host-cell (and many other organisms') enzyme, not a specific marker of HIV infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ordinary RNA polymerase is a host-cell enzyme used broadly in transcription, not a specific marker of HIV infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase is the correct, established marker, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that reverse transcriptase activity in blood is used as a marker of HIV infection.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Paramyxovirus is the RNA exception among DNA viruses
questions.question: All of the following are DNA viruses EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS a DNA virus). Parvovirus is a single-stranded DNA virus, one of the group, not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. Paramyxoviridae is the RNA-genome exception when it appears alongside DNA virus families such as Parvo, Herpes and Pox in an exam list, despite superficially resembling the others in that list. Paramyxoviruses (measles, mumps, respiratory syncytial virus) are enveloped, helical-symmetry RNA viruses, structurally unlike the DNA virus families listed here. This item tests recognizing the one virus that breaks an otherwise consistent DNA-virus pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a DNA virus). Herpesvirus is a double-stranded DNA virus, one of the group, not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS a DNA virus). "Pix virus" is a printed typo for Poxvirus, a double-stranded DNA virus, one of the group, not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize Paramyxovirus as the RNA-genome exception when it appears in an otherwise DNA-virus list.

questions.title: Plaque assay quantitates infectious virus titer
questions.question: Which of the following can be used to quantitate the titer of infectious viruses?

explanations.A: Correct. The plaque assay quantitates the titer of infectious virus particles by counting the discrete zones of cell lysis ("plaques") that form in a susceptible cell monolayer, each plaque arising from a single infectious virion. This makes it a direct measure of infectivity, unlike methods that count total viral particles regardless of whether each is capable of infecting a cell. The plaque assay remains a standard reference method for viral titer determination in virology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Electron microscopy visualizes viral particles directly but does not by itself distinguish infectious from non-infectious particles, so it does not quantitate infectious titer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hemagglutination measures total viral particle count (via red-cell agglutination), including non-infectious particles, not specifically infectious titer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PCR measures genome copy number, not infectious particle count, since it cannot distinguish an intact infectious virion from free or defective viral nucleic acid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Enzyme immunoassay detects viral antigen or antibody, not infectivity, so it does not quantitate infectious titer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the plaque assay as the method used to quantitate the titer of infectious virus particles.

questions.title: Capsid proteins protect the viral genome from nucleases
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding virus morphology is true?

options.A: All RNA viruses are spherical in shape
options.C: Some viruses with DNA genome contain nucleus
options.D: Viral surface proteins protect viral genome from nucleases
options.E: Helical nucleocapsid are found with single stranded DNA virus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Not all RNA viruses are spherical; capsid symmetry varies (icosahedral, helical or complex) across both RNA and DNA virus families.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No virus has a flagellum; flagella are a structure of certain motile bacteria and eukaryotic cells, not viruses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A virus's own particle never contains a nucleus; a nucleus is a structure of the host cell it infects, not of the virus itself.
explanations.D: Correct. The capsid's tightly packed surface proteins protect the enclosed viral genome against inactivation by host nucleases. This protective function, together with mediating attachment to host-cell receptors, is one of the capsid's core structural roles. It applies broadly across DNA and RNA viruses, naked and enveloped alike, since the capsid always directly encases the genome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Helical nucleocapsid symmetry is classically associated with single-stranded RNA viruses (for example rhabdovirus, paramyxovirus), not single-stranded DNA viruses.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral surface (capsid) proteins protect the viral genome against inactivation by host nucleases.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Prion contains no detectable nucleic acid
questions.question: Prion is an atypical virus that contain which of the following?

options.E: Host cell DNA Instead of viral DNA

explanations.A: Incorrect. Circular RNA without a protein coat describes a viroid, not a prion, which by definition has no nucleic acid at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carrying multiple plasmid copies describes a different, unrelated genetic element, not the prion's defining feature.
explanations.C: Correct. A prion is an infectious protein particle that contains no detectable nucleic acid of any kind -- no DNA, no RNA, no plasmid. This is what makes it "atypical" as an infectious agent when compared to a virus, which always has DNA or RNA. Because it has no nucleic acid to replicate, a prion propagates instead by inducing a conformational (misfolding) change in the host's own normal cellular protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Double-stranded RNA describes certain conventional virus genomes (for example reoviruses), not a prion, which has no nucleic acid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Containing host cell DNA instead of viral DNA describes a pseudovirion, a different phenomenon from a prion's complete absence of nucleic acid.

questions.learning_objective: State that a prion contains no detectable nucleic acid.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Virus size range 20-300 nm
questions.question: Which of the following statements best describe virus?

options.B: Can be grown on blood agar

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viruses are obligate INTRAcellular parasites, not extracellular; they can only replicate inside a living host cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blood agar is a bacteriological growth medium; viruses require living host cells, not an inert nutrient medium, and cannot be cultured on blood agar.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A virus's genome is either DNA or RNA, never both together, so this statement misdescribes viral genetics.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viruses lack the bacterial-specific cell-wall and metabolic targets antibiotics act on, so they are not susceptible to antibiotics.
explanations.E: Correct. Viruses are typically very small, ranging from about 20 to 300 nm, small enough to require electron microscopy for direct visualization -- with poxvirus near the upper end and parvovirus near the lower end of that range. This size range, together with being obligate intracellular parasites and antibiotic-insusceptible, is one of the best single descriptive statements about viruses as a group. It is this small size that necessitated the development of electron microscopy before viruses could be directly visualized.

questions.learning_objective: State that viruses are typically 20-300 nm in size, among their general defining properties.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viral replication requires host cell macromolecules
questions.question: Viral replication?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viral replication does not occur by binary fission; a virus is assembled from pre-made components inside a host cell rather than growing and splitting as a whole organism the way a bacterium does.
explanations.B: Correct. Viral replication requires the host cell's own macromolecules -- ribosomes, enzymes, nucleotide precursors, energy -- because a virus has no independent metabolic or protein-synthesis machinery of its own. This dependence on hijacked host processes is a defining feature of obligate intracellular parasitism. It is also why viral replication can proceed only inside living host cells, never in cell-free media.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because replication depends on host processes rather than the bacterial-type targets antibiotics act on, viral replication is not prevented by antibiotics.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viral replication cannot occur in a cell-free synthetic medium; it requires living host cells to supply the macromolecules and machinery a virus lacks on its own.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral replication requires host cell macromolecules, since a virus has no independent metabolic machinery.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Smallpox has complex capsid symmetry
questions.question: Capsid symmetry found in smallpox virus is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Helical symmetry is classically associated with enveloped RNA viruses, not smallpox (a DNA poxvirus).
explanations.B: Correct. Smallpox virus (variola), a poxvirus, has complex capsid symmetry -- an irregular, brick-shaped structure not reducible to either the icosahedral or helical form. This complex symmetry is the classic distinguishing structural feature of the poxvirus family among DNA viruses. It reflects poxvirus's unusually large, complex virion, consistent with its status as the largest medically important virus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Icosahedral symmetry describes most other DNA viruses (for example herpesvirus, adenovirus), but poxvirus is specifically the complex-symmetry exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Complex" is the correct, standard answer, so "none of these" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that smallpox (poxvirus) has complex capsid symmetry.

questions.title: Viruses do not multiply by binary fission
questions.question: One of the following statements is not true for viruses?

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS true). A virus's genome is indeed either DNA or RNA, never both, so this statement is true of viruses.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS true). Viruses lack mitochondria, along with every other organelle, since they are not true cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS true). A virus does contain a protein coat, the capsid, surrounding its nucleic acid genome.
explanations.D: Correct (the false statement). Viruses do NOT multiply by binary fission; that mechanism is specific to bacteria and other cellular organisms that grow and split as a whole cell. A virus instead multiplies by assembling new virions from separately synthesized components (nucleic acid replication and protein synthesis, followed by assembly) inside a host cell. This distinction -- assembly versus binary fission -- is a key structural difference between viral and bacterial replication.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that viruses do not multiply by binary fission, unlike the other listed true statements about viral properties.

questions.title: Envelope is not made of small protein subunits
questions.question: All of the following about viral envelope is true EXCEPT?

options.A: Formed from the host cell during budding
options.D: Formed from the membranes of host cell

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS true). The envelope's lipid portion is indeed acquired from the host cell during the budding process.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS true). Because the envelope is lipid, it is susceptible to disruption by alcohol and other lipid solvents, which is true of enveloped viruses.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). The viral envelope's protein component consists of larger glycoprotein spikes (peplomers) embedded in the lipid bilayer, a structurally different arrangement from the capsid's own small protein subunits, the capsomeres. Describing the envelope as made of "small protein subunits" confuses it with the capsid, whose capsomeres are the small subunits. This distinction matters because it is the envelope's larger glycoproteins, not capsomeres, that mediate host-cell attachment for enveloped viruses and drive antigenic variation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS true). The envelope is formed from the membranes of the host cell (plasma or nuclear membrane) during budding, consistent with option A.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the envelope's larger glycoprotein spikes from the capsid's small capsomere subunits.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Capsomere is an individual capsid subunit
questions.question: Which of the following statements are true about the capsomeres?

options.A: It is an individual unit of the capsid
options.B: It is a viral protein for replication
options.C: It is a unit of nucleic acid in viruses

explanations.A: Correct. A capsomere is the individual, small protein subunit that assembles together with many others to build the capsid. This is distinct from a nucleic acid unit or a replication-related viral protein, and distinct from the envelope's own larger glycoprotein spikes. Multiple capsomeres arranged in a repeating geometric pattern give the capsid its overall symmetry (icosahedral, helical or complex).
explanations.B: Incorrect. A capsomere is a structural capsid subunit, not a protein involved in viral genome replication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A capsomere is a protein subunit, not a unit of nucleic acid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since options B and C are each individually incorrect, "all of the above" cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a capsomere as an individual protein subunit of the capsid.

questions.title: Capsid does not absorb nutrients
questions.question: What is not function of capsid?

options.A: Protects viral genome against inactivation by nuclease
options.C: Participate in the attachment of the virus to the susceptible host
options.D: They induce antibodies and activate Tc

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS a function). Protecting the genome against nuclease inactivation is one of the capsid's genuine true functions.
explanations.B: Correct. Absorbing nutrients by active transport is NOT a function of the capsid, or of any part of a virus, because a virus has no independent metabolism -- it is an obligate intracellular parasite that depends entirely on the host cell's own metabolic machinery once inside. This is the one option in the list that describes a metabolic activity, which no viral structure performs. The capsid's true functions are all structural or immunological (protection, attachment, antigenicity), never metabolic.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a function). Participating in attachment of the virus to susceptible host-cell receptors is one of the capsid's genuine true functions.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS a function). Inducing antibodies (antigenicity) and activating cytotoxic T cells are genuine immunological consequences of the capsid's antigenic protein surface.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that a virus, and its capsid, cannot absorb nutrients by active transport, since it has no independent metabolism.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Enveloped-virus serotypes vary by envelope protein, not capsid protein
questions.question: What is wrong about virus?

options.A: Can't generate energy outside the cell
options.C: Variation in capsid protein is responsible for different serotypes in enveloped virus

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS true). A virus cannot generate energy outside a host cell, since it has no independent metabolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS true). A virus is indeed an obligate intracellular parasite, replicating only inside a living host cell.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). For enveloped viruses specifically, antigenic variation that produces different serotypes is driven by variation in the envelope's own surface glycoproteins, not by variation in the underlying capsid protein, since the envelope is the outermost, immunologically exposed layer. Attributing serotype differences among enveloped viruses to capsid protein variation is therefore the incorrect statement here. This distinction matters clinically, since vaccine antigen choice for enveloped viruses targets envelope glycoproteins, the actual site of antigenic drift.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS true). A virus does need a host cell to replicate, consistent with being an obligate intracellular parasite.

questions.learning_objective: State that serotype variation among enveloped viruses arises from envelope protein variation, not capsid protein variation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Prions cannot multiply the way viruses do
questions.question: All of the following about Prions are true EXCEPT?

options.C: They are responsible for transmitting spongi form encephalopathy

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS true). A prion is indeed an infectious protein particle, its most basic defining feature.
explanations.B: Correct (the false statement). Because a prion lacks nucleic acid entirely, it cannot "multiply" in the sense a virus does through nucleic acid replication and protein synthesis. Instead it propagates by inducing a conformational (misfolding) change in the host's own normal cellular protein, converting it into the abnormal, infectious conformation. Describing this process as ordinary "multiplication" is the false statement here, since it implies a replicative mechanism prions do not have.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS true). Prions are indeed responsible for transmitting spongiform encephalopathies (for example Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease), a genuine true statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS true). Because they have no nucleic acid, prions correspondingly lack any genes, a genuine true statement.

questions.learning_objective: State that prions cannot multiply by nucleic-acid-based replication, unlike a virus, but instead propagate by protein misfolding.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Capsid is composed of capsomers
questions.question: The capsid is composed of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peplomers are the envelope's glycoprotein spikes, a component of the envelope, not the capsid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nucleic acid is the genome the capsid surrounds and protects, not a component of the capsid itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The capsid is composed of capsomeres, individual small protein subunits that assemble together in a repeating geometric pattern to build the complete capsid structure. The number and arrangement of capsomeres determines the capsid's overall symmetry (icosahedral, helical or complex). This is distinct from the envelope, which is composed instead of a lipid bilayer studded with larger glycoprotein spikes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The envelope is a separate structure surrounding the capsid in enveloped viruses; it is not what the capsid itself is composed of.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Glucose is a simple sugar, not a structural component of the capsid.

questions.learning_objective: State that the capsid is composed of capsomeres.

questions.title: Virus multiplies in living tissue
questions.question: Virus multiplies in?

explanations.A: Correct. A virus can only multiply inside living tissue -- living host cells -- because it has no independent metabolic or protein-synthesis machinery of its own and must hijack the host cell's own macromolecules and machinery. This is a defining feature of obligate intracellular parasitism, and it is why viral culture in the laboratory requires living cell lines or embryonated eggs, not an inert medium. Once host-cell death occurs, ongoing viral replication in that cell also ceases.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A general "culture media" (a cell-free nutrient broth or agar) cannot support viral replication, since a virus requires the specific machinery only a living host cell provides.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dead tissue cannot support viral replication, since the host cell's own metabolic and synthetic machinery is no longer functioning.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Soil is an inert, non-living environment and cannot support viral replication.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus multiplies only in living tissue (living host cells).

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viruses use host, not viral, tRNA and ribosomes
questions.question: Which of the following statements about viruses are NOT TRUE?

options.B: The virus' nucleic acid is surrounded by a protein coat
options.C: Viruses multiply inside living cells using viral mRNA, viral tRNA and viral ribosomes
options.D: For DNA viruses (except pox viruses) assembly occurs in the nucleus. In RNA viruses and pox viruses assembly occurs in the cytoplasm
options.E: Early viral proteins are enzymes required for replication of the viral genome

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS true). Viruses do contain either DNA or RNA, a genuine true statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS true). The virus's nucleic acid is indeed surrounded by a protein coat, the capsid, a genuine true statement.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). A virus multiplies inside a living cell by directing the synthesis of viral proteins using its own viral mRNA, but that mRNA is translated using the HOST cell's own tRNA and ribosomes -- a virus encodes neither its own tRNA nor its own ribosomes. Claiming that viruses use "viral tRNA and viral ribosomes" is therefore the false statement, since only the mRNA is virus-encoded and the entire translation apparatus is borrowed from the host. This is a key reason a virus is considered an obligate intracellular parasite dependent on host machinery.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS true). DNA viruses (except poxvirus) do assemble in the nucleus, while RNA viruses and poxvirus assemble in the cytoplasm, a genuine true statement consistent with the general replication-site rule.
explanations.E: Incorrect (it IS true). Early viral proteins being enzymes required for genome replication is a genuine true statement about the typical sequence of viral gene expression.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize that a virus uses the host cell's tRNA and ribosomes, not its own, even though its mRNA is virus-encoded.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Naked viruses are non-enveloped
questions.question: Naked viruses are?

options.D: Viruses are genetically deficient and so incapable of producing infections daughter virion
options.E: Infective agents with protein free, with low molecular weight RNA

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Enveloped" is the opposite of naked; a naked virus by definition lacks an envelope.
explanations.B: Correct. "Naked" and "non-enveloped" are synonyms describing the same structural fact: a naked virus consists of the nucleocapsid only, genome plus capsid, with no surrounding lipid envelope. This structural difference is why naked viruses are generally more resistant than enveloped viruses to lipid solvents, detergents and drying. The term "naked" specifically emphasizes the absence of the envelope layer that would otherwise cover the capsid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A prion is an entirely different infectious agent, a protein particle with no nucleic acid at all, not a description of envelope status.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes a defective virus (missing genes needed for replication), a genetic deficiency unrelated to envelope status.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This describes a viroid (uncoated circular RNA, no protein), a different infectious agent entirely, not the definition of "naked virus."

questions.learning_objective: State that "naked" and "non-enveloped" are synonymous terms for a virus lacking an envelope.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Prions are protein-only infectious particles
questions.question: Prions are?

options.A: Viruses are genetically deficient and so incapable of producing infections daughter virion
options.B: Infective agents with protein free, with low molecular weight RNA
options.C: Protein infections particles, lack detectable nucleic acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes a defective virus, one missing genes needed for independent replication -- a different concept, since a defective virus does still have (incomplete) nucleic acid, unlike a prion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes a viroid (a protein-free, low-molecular-weight circular RNA), the exact opposite composition of a prion, which is protein-only with no RNA at all.
explanations.C: Correct. A prion is an infectious protein particle that contains no detectable nucleic acid of any kind. This protein-only composition is what distinguishes it from a virus (always has DNA or RNA), a viroid (RNA, no protein) and a defective virus (has incomplete nucleic acid). Because it lacks nucleic acid, a prion propagates by inducing host-protein misfolding rather than by nucleic-acid-based replication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extrachromosomal genetic elements describes a plasmid, a DNA element distinct from and unrelated to a prion's protein-only composition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A defective virus still has (incomplete) nucleic acid and requires a helper virus to replicate; a prion has no nucleic acid at all and is not a virus.

questions.learning_objective: Define a prion as an infectious protein particle lacking detectable nucleic acid.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viral genetic material is DNA or RNA
questions.question: The genetic material in virus is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "DNA only" is too narrow; many viruses (for example influenza, HIV, poliovirus) instead carry an RNA genome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "RNA only" is too narrow; many viruses (for example herpesvirus, adenovirus, poxvirus) instead carry a DNA genome.
explanations.C: Correct. Every virus carries exactly one type of nucleic acid as its genome -- either DNA or RNA -- and never both together. This single-nucleic-acid-type rule is one of the defining structural features separating viruses from cellular organisms, which carry both DNA and RNA. It underlies the basic DNA-virus/RNA-virus classification scheme used throughout virology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Selecting "DNA and RNA" incorrectly implies a virus carries both nucleic acid types simultaneously, when in fact every virus has exactly one.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus's genetic material is either DNA or RNA, never both.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Poxvirus has complex symmetry
questions.question: Which of the following viruses have a complex symmetry?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alphavirus (an enveloped RNA virus family) has icosahedral capsid symmetry, not complex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Morbillivirus (printed "Mobillivirus", the measles-virus genus) has helical capsid symmetry, not complex.
explanations.C: Correct. Poxvirus is the classic example of complex capsid symmetry among medically important virus families -- an irregular, brick-shaped structure not reducible to icosahedral or helical form. This complex symmetry reflects poxvirus's unusually large virion, and it is a distinguishing structural feature that also explains why poxvirus can encode its own complete cytoplasmic replication machinery. Smallpox virus (variola) is the standard example used to illustrate this symmetry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parvovirus, a small DNA virus, has icosahedral capsid symmetry, not complex.

questions.learning_objective: Identify poxvirus as the virus family with complex capsid symmetry among the listed options.

questions.title: Prions are infectious protein particles without nucleic acid
questions.question: Prions are?

options.A: Infectious protein particles without nucleic acid
options.B: Contain host cell DNA instead of viral DNA
options.C: Viruses that replicate if the cells are co infected with helper virus

explanations.A: Correct. A prion is an infectious protein particle that contains no detectable nucleic acid of any kind. This protein-only definition is the core fact distinguishing a prion from every other infectious agent covered in this chapter (viruses, viroids, defective viruses), all of which carry some form of nucleic acid. Because it lacks nucleic acid, a prion propagates by inducing host-protein misfolding rather than by replicating in the conventional sense.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Containing host cell DNA instead of viral DNA describes a pseudovirion, a different phenomenon involving mispackaged host DNA, not a prion's complete absence of nucleic acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A virus that replicates only when the cell is co-infected with a helper virus describes a defective virus, which does have (incomplete) nucleic acid, unlike a prion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "An intact infectious viral particle" describes a virion, which by definition contains nucleic acid; a prion is specifically defined by the absence of any nucleic acid.

questions.learning_objective: Define a prion as an infectious protein particle without nucleic acid.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Defective viruses need a helper virus to replicate
questions.question: Viruses that can replicate if the cells are co infected with a helper virus called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A prion is protein-only with no nucleic acid, an entirely different agent from a virus that requires a helper for replication.
explanations.B: Correct. A defective virus is a virus particle missing one or more genes necessary for a complete, independent replication cycle; such a virus can only replicate and spread if the same cell is co-infected with a helper virus that supplies the missing function. This rescue mechanism, in which the helper virus's gene products complement the defective virus's missing ones, is called complementation. Hepatitis D virus (which requires simultaneous hepatitis B virus infection) is a clinically important real-world example of a defective virus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pseudovirion is a particle containing mispackaged host nucleic acid instead of viral genome, a different phenomenon from needing a helper virus for replication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A lytic phage is a bacteriophage that lyses its bacterial host after replication, an unrelated concept to helper-virus dependence.

questions.learning_objective: Define a defective virus as one requiring helper-virus co-infection to replicate.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Virus is made of protein coat and nucleic acid
questions.question: A virus is made up of?

options.D: Nucleic acid, cell membrane and cell wall

explanations.A: Incorrect. A virus has no ribosome of its own; it must borrow the host cell's ribosomes to translate its mRNA.
explanations.B: Correct. A virion is a complete virus particle consisting of a DNA or RNA genome surrounded by a protein capsid -- the two universal components every virus has. An enveloped virus additionally has a lipid envelope around this nucleocapsid, but the protein coat plus nucleic acid combination is the minimum, universal composition. This basic composition is what a naked (non-enveloped) virus consists of in full.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A virus has no cell membrane of its own; that is a structure of true cells, not viruses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A virus has neither a cell membrane nor a cell wall of its own; both are structures of true cells, not viruses.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus's basic composition is a protein coat (capsid) surrounding a nucleic acid genome.

questions.title: Reassortment requires a segmented genome
questions.question: Genetic reassortment occurs is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A viroid has a single, uncoated circular RNA genome, not a segmented one, so it cannot undergo reassortment.
explanations.B: Correct. Genetic reassortment is the exchange of whole genome segments between two different strains of a segmented-genome virus co-infecting the same host cell, producing a hybrid progeny virus. It can only happen in viruses whose genome is naturally divided into separate segments, such as influenza's eight-segment RNA genome. Reassortment is the mechanism underlying antigenic shift, the abrupt, major antigenic change distinct from the gradual point-mutation-driven antigenic drift.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A defective virus's problem is missing genes, not genome segmentation, and reassortment specifically requires a segmented genome to exchange, which a defective virus does not define.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A host-range mutant is defined by an altered ability to infect a particular host or cell type, not by genome segmentation or reassortment.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A prion has no nucleic acid at all, so it cannot undergo genetic reassortment, which requires exchanging genome segments.

questions.learning_objective: State that genetic reassortment requires a segmented viral genome.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Phenotypic masking: genome packaged in another virus's capsid
questions.question: Viral genome of one virus that may be encapsulated in the capsid of the second virus is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A point mutation is a single-nucleotide change in a genome, an unrelated concept to one virus's genome being packaged in another virus's capsid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exaltation is one virus enhancing another's growth, a functional interaction distinct from genome/capsid mismatching.
explanations.C: Correct. Phenotypic masking (phenotypic mixing) occurs when two related viruses co-infect the same cell and the genome of one virus becomes packaged inside capsid proteins contributed by the other. The resulting particle carries the genetic information of one parent virus but the surface phenotype (and initial host-cell tropism) of the other. It changes only the outer coat borrowed for one generation, leaving the genome itself unaltered, unlike reassortment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interference is one virus suppressing another's replication, the opposite kind of interaction from genome/capsid packaging.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Reassortment is the exchange of whole genome segments, an actual genetic change, unlike phenotypic masking, which changes only the coat, not the genome.

questions.learning_objective: Define phenotypic masking as one virus's genome packaged in capsid proteins contributed by a co-infecting second virus.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Complementation allows defective viruses to replicate
questions.question: A process that allows defective viruses to replicate and spread is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Recombination is an exchange of genetic sequence between two genomes, a different mechanism from the missing-function rescue described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reassortment is the exchange of whole genome segments between segmented-genome viruses, an unrelated mechanism from rescuing a defective virus's missing function.
explanations.C: Correct. Complementation is the process by which a helper virus's gene products supply the function a defective virus's own genome is missing, allowing the defective virus to replicate and spread despite its own incomplete genome. This rescue process is distinct from recombination (exchange of genetic sequence) or interference (one virus suppressing another's replication, the opposite effect). Hepatitis D virus's dependence on simultaneous hepatitis B virus infection is a clinically relevant real-world example of complementation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interference is one virus suppressing another's replication, the opposite effect from rescuing a defective virus's replication.

questions.learning_objective: Name complementation as the process by which a helper virus rescues a defective virus's replication.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Conditional-lethal mutants: permissive vs restrictive conditions
questions.question: Mutations that can multiply under some conditions but not under other conditions are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plaque-size mutant is defined by an altered diameter of the lysis zone it produces, not by permissive-vs-restrictive replication conditions.
explanations.B: Correct. A conditional-lethal mutant is a virus mutant that can multiply under some (permissive) conditions but not under other (restrictive) conditions -- temperature-sensitive mutants are the classic example, replicating at a lower permissive temperature but not at a higher restrictive one. This condition-dependent replication pattern is the defining phenotype of this mutant class. Such mutants are valuable research tools because they can be propagated under permissive conditions and then studied under restrictive ones.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A host-range mutant is defined by an altered ability to infect a particular host or cell type, not by permissive-vs-restrictive conditions for the same host.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A drug-resistant mutant is defined by continued replication in the presence of an antiviral drug that would inhibit wild-type virus, a different phenotype from condition-dependent replication.

questions.learning_objective: Define a conditional-lethal mutant as one that replicates only under permissive, not restrictive, conditions.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Plaque-size mutants alter the lysis zone diameter
questions.question: Mutations that induce changes in the diameter of the zone of viral lysis in infected cell monolayers are?

explanations.A: Correct. A plaque-size mutant is a mutant that induces a change in the diameter of the zone of viral lysis (the plaque) it produces in an infected cell monolayer. This phenotype is used to distinguish mutant from wild-type virus by visual plaque morphology, without reference to temperature sensitivity or drug resistance at all. Plaque-size differences are readily scored during the same plaque assay used to quantitate infectious viral titer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A conditional-lethal mutant is defined by permissive-vs-restrictive replication conditions, not by an altered plaque diameter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A host-range mutant is defined by an altered ability to infect a particular host or cell type, not by plaque diameter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A drug-resistant mutant is defined by continued replication in the presence of an antiviral drug, not by plaque diameter.

questions.learning_objective: Define a plaque-size mutant as one that alters the diameter of the lysis zone it produces in a cell monolayer.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Exaltation: one virus enhances another's growth
questions.question: Exaltation means?

options.A: One virus enhances the growth of the other virus

explanations.A: Correct. Exaltation is the phenomenon in which one virus, through co-infection, enhances the growth (replication) of a second, different virus in the same cell -- the reverse of interference, in which one virus instead suppresses another's replication. It is not a mutation, and it does not itself involve genetic reassortment of the viral genome; it is a functional interaction between two co-infecting viruses, not a change to either genome. Exaltation and interference together illustrate that co-infecting viruses can either help or hinder one another's replication.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nonsense mutation is a specific type of point mutation that creates a premature stop codon, an unrelated genome-sequence change, not exaltation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Genetic reassortment is the exchange of whole genome segments, an actual genetic change; exaltation instead describes a functional growth-enhancing interaction that leaves each virus's genome unchanged.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A point mutation is a single-nucleotide genome change, an unrelated concept to one virus enhancing another's growth.

questions.learning_objective: Define exaltation as one virus enhancing the growth of another co-infecting virus.
